title: [HashiCorp] Building a secure foundation for AI on Kubernetes with HashiCorp Vault
summary: AI is moving beyond experimentation and into production, but security controls aren’t necessarily keeping pace. Recent IBM research shows 48% of surveyed executives say their organizations lack adequate protection for model inference and live AI usage, while 56% say the same about AI development and training. As organizations move AI applications, models, and autonomous agents into production environments orchestrated by platforms such as Kubernetes, closing that security gap requires looking beyond the AI model itself.This shift is reflected in team priorities and thought leadership, including the agenda at this year’s KubeCon. Moving a model from demo to production introduces challenges across compute, GPU utilization, model serving, networking, storage, observability, cost and most importantly, security. Autonomous AI agents add the consideration: how can workloads safely and securely interact with infrastructure, APIs, tools, and data. For platform and security teams, that changes the conversation. Securing AI on Kubernetes isn't only about protecting a model or application. It requires securing the infrastructure underneath it, including the data stored by Kubernetes, the identities and certificates workloads use to establish trust, and the credentials applications need to access other systems. Protect the Kubernetes foundation beneath AI workloadsKubernetes uses etcd as its backing store for cluster data, which can include Kubernetes Secrets and other sensitive configuration associated with workloads running in the cluster. By default, the Kubernetes API server stores unencrypted representations of resources in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured. For organizations running sensitive workloads, including AI applications, protecting this data adds an important layer of defense if unauthorized access to the underlying storage occurs. Vault Kubernetes Key Management reduces this risk by integrating Kubernetes encryption with the Vault Transit secrets engine. The vault-kube-kms process exposes the Kubernetes KMS v2 interface and connects the Kubernetes API server to Vault, where the Transit engine is used for cryptographic key wrapping operations.With Vault 2.2, Vault Kubernetes Key Management advances to full support for general Kubernetes deployment. This approach helps organizations centralize control over the keys protecting Kubernetes data rather than managing encryption independently for every cluster.For production AI environments, Kubernetes hosts far more than just the model itself. Model-serving infrastructure, AI gateways, MCP servers, agents, application services, and the configuration required to operate them may all depend on the Kubernetes control plane. Securing AI starts with securing the platform it runs on.Automate trust with Vault and cert-managerAs cloud native architectures become more distributed, applications increasingly rely on certificates to establish trusted, encrypted connections between workloads. Consider an agentic application running on Kubernetes. An AI agent might communicate with an MCP server, which connects to an internal API, which in turn accesses a database or another service. Each connection creates another trust relationship that platform teams need to secure.This web of interdependent services makes automated certificate lifecycle management a critical part of the Kubernetes security model.A new external Vault issuer for cert-manager means application developers can continue requesting certificates using standard cert-manager Certificate resources, while VSO 2.0 sends approved certificate requests to Vault PKI for signing. The approach also reuses VSO's existing authentication and client infrastructure rather than requiring teams to establish a separate Vault integration for certificate management. And with shrinking certificate lifecycles, integrations with Vault and automations in it are even more relevant for teams when it comes to managing certificates. The benefit is not a new certificate workflow. It leverages familiar Kubernetes-native workflows, so that teams that have standardized on cert-manager can continue using these familiar workflows, while bringing certificate signing under centralized Vault PKI controls. This centralized control helps platform teams automate workload trust without asking every application team to learn a separate security process, ensuring identity-based access and secure execution supporting autonomous workload access. Keep secrets synchronized as workloads changeSecret delivery is only part of the problem. Credentials also rotate, applications scale, and configurations change. Common polling approaches can leave a window for downtime between when a credential changes and when a workload receives that change.Vault 2.2 expands Vault Secrets Operator instant updates. VSO 1.6 can immediately deliver changes for dynamic, auto-rotating, and manually rotated database, KV, Azure, and LDAP secrets. VSO reconciliation through Vault event notifications is triggered immediately on secrets changes. Reducing the gap between credential rotation and availability helps security controls keep pace with the applications they protect, which is necessary for dynamic applications, including AI and agentic workloads that interact with multiple services and must move securely at machine speed. Give workloads secure access without the full Vault server footprintSecrets present another challenge. Applications, AI services, and autonomous agents all need credentials to access databases, APIs, cloud services, model endpoints, and other tools at runtime. But the component consuming those secrets doesn't need all the functionality required to operate a Vault server.Vault 2.2 introduces Vault Client. Vault Client packages Vault Agent, Vault Proxy, and a limited set of Vault CLI commands without requiring the complete Vault server binary. Not all organizations have embraced Kubernetes secrets. For deployments and secrets that require additional isolation or more-limited secrets visibility, Vault Agent and Agent Sidecar Injector are now available in a smaller footprint for workloads that need client-side Vault functionality while establishing a clear separation between the capabilities required to operate Vault and those required to consume services from it. For increasingly dynamic cloud native environments, that distinction can help simplify how Vault functionality is deployed alongside applications.Build a security foundation for cloud native AIBut the bigger story is not any individual Kubernetes integration. It's how these capabilities work across different layers of the cloud native stack:Protect cluster data: Vault Kubernetes Key Management connects Kubernetes KMS with Vault Transit to protect Kubernetes data stored in etcd. Establish workload trust: The Vault issuer for cert-manager brings Vault PKI into familiar Kubernetes certificate workflows.Keep credentials current: VSO instant updates help Kubernetes applications receive secret changes as they happen.Secure runtime access: Vault Client provides a lightweight way for workloads to use common Vault client functionality. Together, these capabilities point toward a consistent security model: Kubernetes-native workflows for developers and platform teams, backed by centralized controls for secrets, certificates, and encryption.Secure what comes after the AI demoOrganizations focused on securing AI at scale are challenged beyond just getting a model to run securely in production. Teams need the infrastructure and operational practices to serve models, operate agents, secure workloads, control access, and connect the growing number of systems surrounding AI applications. Security must evolve alongside that infrastructure.As organizations bring AI applications and autonomous workloads onto Kubernetes, Vault can help provide the security foundation beneath them, protecting Kubernetes data, automating workload trust, and giving applications secure access to the credentials they need. Ready to secure your Kubernetes workloads? Explore the HashiCorp Vault Kubernetes developer documentation to get started.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
summary: On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.What we know about ruby2shellRuby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposedHTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.Who is affectedConditionDetailsRuby versionRuby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.FrameworkRails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.Bundled softwareAs of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.Six more Ruby flaws in the same releaseRuby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.How Cloudflare WAF protects youUpgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.New managed rules, on for every customerBoth rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.Rule descriptionRule IDRulesetDefault actionRuby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-1328257328f23691e44b07892ebd25b19210f1Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockRuby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-1328251afa543a1ed84893b01df04c34402c88Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockRuby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px8660e37e86444f9f9267ba22e9855f05Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockRuby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px6defac6a52334542adf4a162daf25922Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockOn the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.What the WAF cannot seeA WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls.Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request.Adding defense in depth with WAF attack scoreMemory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.Impact on Cloudflare infrastructureCloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor.Patch nowruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
summary: On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.What we know about phpAfterShellPHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.The other critical flawsThe same releases fix six more critical vulnerabilities. Each one needs a specific configuration to be exploitable:CVEComponentImpactConditionsCVE-2026-129289PHP-FPMAn unauthenticated attacker can smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code as the worker.A front end that reuses backend FastCGI connections (nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy), an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end, and the path of an existing PHP script.CVE-2026-115560Session serializerObject injection through a mismatch between session serializers. First covered in our php2shell briefing, now fixed.Session upload progress enabled. PHP widened the scope: applications, pools or command-line jobs that use different serializers and share a session store are affected.CVE-2026-129496Timezone cacheUse-after-free that can crash a fresh worker and possibly run code. PHP demonstrated code execution locally with known memory addresses.Non-thread-safe builds where a startup diagnostic has been written to a PHP error log file.CVE-2026-129481Session shutdownUse-after-free, described by PHP as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619. No code execution demonstrated.PHP 8.3 and later.CVE-2026-129474Fatal error backtracesUse-after-free in magic method backtraces.PHP 8.5 and later, where fatal error backtraces are enabled by default. Setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1, the php.ini-production default, blocks the demonstrated attack.CVE-2026-129182Fatal error backtracesUse-after-free. No code execution demonstrated.PHP 8.5, specific path-level settings, and an Apache per-directory configuration or front end that produces an early diagnostic.Who is affectedThe vulnerable versions are PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13, and the 8.6.0 release candidates. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw.PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell, but PHP says CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560.Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number. Check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.How Cloudflare WAF protects youPHP runs a large share of the web, often inside content management systems, plugins, and container images that teams do not update directly. Patching every PHP runtime takes time. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.phpAfterShell: protection on every planWe released the original PHP remote code execution rules in an emergency release on October 21, 2026, after the php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed. We extended them to CVE-2026-115560 on October 23 and refined them several times in the following weeks, based in part on reports from security researchers who took part in a PHP Capture the Flag (CTF) challenge.phpAfterShell shares an attack technique with php2shell: an attacker plants serialized PHP data in session storage and waits for PHP to deserialize it. Because of that overlap, the existing rule already matched part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before disclosure. On November 19, we updated the rule's detection logic to cover phpAfterShell and added CVE-2026-126714 to its description.Rule descriptionRule IDRulesetDefault actionPHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714) #619373a83abb840e18ab3ce5a7975ce1bCloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockPHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714) #64148ae686fdb4d01be673fab9d9c073dCloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockFree plan customers do not need to take any action. On paid plans, the rule is active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.New rules for PHP-FPM and SOAP flawsThe three new rules are part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee) and are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans.Rule descriptionRule IDDefault actionPHP-FPM - CVE:CVE-2026-1292898ef1c34a424b4ccfa6f6fe186c6f42b2LogPHP SOAP - CVE:CVE-2026-153535c5a9d6397e44837a3214b5ba54028d4LogPHP SOAP - CVE:CVE-2026-12950600a23de67a684876ba67c5d44521b819LogTo review their matches, go to Security > Analytics > Events and filter by rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for the CVE identifier and set the rule action to Block, or you can refer to the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules configuration.What the WAF cannot seeA WAF can block an exploit when the malicious data arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them.Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network.Adding defense in depth with WAF attack scoreWAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans.Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score:Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score.Deploy protections and patchYou can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide. In short:Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. On paid plans, make sure the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and that the PHP Remote Code Execution Attack #6 rule is set to Block.Review the new rules and switch them to Block. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block.Layer attack score. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version that serves web requests. After upgrading, check that no php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.Apply interim mitigations if you cannot upgrade right away. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and limit the untrusted data you store in sessions. Turn off FastCGI connection reuse. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Fix configuration errors that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks. These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your PHP deployments and check each one against all seven critical CVEs, see the phpAfterShell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire.Update every PHP runtime nowphpAfterShell turns an interrupted file write in PHP's default session handler into a path to code execution, and it arrived in the same release as six other critical flaws. With technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow. Cloudflare WAF blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns for every customer, including the Free plan, and paid plans have new rules for the PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws. The fix is still to upgrade PHP and restart the services that use it.

title: [Pulumi] Trigger Pulumi Agents from Infrastructure Events
summary: Pulumi Agents can start work automatically in response to a Pulumi event or a webhook. With a trigger, you can give an agent a recurring assignment and choose when it should start. For events in Pulumi Cloud, that choice can be as specific as a failed update on a single stack. A failed deployment is one use for a trigger. The agent can read the failed update, identify the affected resource, and post a diagnosis in Slack. That puts the error and a suggested next step in the deployment channel for the team to review. A trigger for failed deployments The example below defines an agent and a trigger in TypeScript. The trigger selects failed updates on checkout/prod and starts an investigation. The agent has read access to the stack’s update history and instructions to report what failed and what to check next. The agent’s instructions describe what you want to learn from each failure. Its roleId determines what it can read. Here, agentRoleId is a configuration key that holds the ID of an existing Pulumi Cloud role with stack:read on checkout/prod. The configuration steps below show how to look up that ID and supply it through Pulumi ESC. import * as pulumi from "@pulumi/pulumi"; import * as service from "@pulumi/pulumiservice"; const config = new pulumi.Config(); const orgName = pulumi.getOrganization(); const agent = new service.api.agents.Definition("troubleshooter", { orgName, name: "deployment-troubleshooter", displayName: "Deployment Troubleshooter", roleId: config.require("agentRoleId"), customInstructions: .join(" "), }); Start a task when an update fails Add the automation to the same program. Its trigger matches three details that Pulumi Cloud records for a stack operation: the stack, the operation, and the result. When an update to checkout/prod finishes with a failed result, Pulumi starts a task for the agent referenced by agent.definitionID. new service.api.AgentAutomationV2("failed-update", { orgName, name: "Investigate failed production updates", kind: "triggered", trigger: { type: "stack_operation", stacks: , operations: , results: , quietPeriodSeconds: 30, }, task: { agentDefinitionId: agent.definitionID, toolExecutionMode: "cloud", message: { type: "user_message", content: "Investigate this failed update." }, }, notificationTargets: , }); The first failure starts the task immediately. The 30-second window lets subsequent matching events join the investigation. The agent reads the update using its Pulumi Cloud role, and Pulumi delivers the findings to the Slack channel in notificationTargets. Configure and deploy Create a TypeScript project named deployment-agents with pulumi new typescript --name deployment-agents, and put both code snippets above in its index.ts. Select a stack for that project in the same Pulumi Cloud organization as checkout/prod. Find the role ID. With a Pulumi account that can list roles in your organization, run the command below. Replace YOUR_ORG with the organization name. The output lists each role’s name and ID. Copy the ID of the role you’ve granted read access to checkout/prod. pulumi api /api/orgs/YOUR_ORG/roles --method GET -F uxPurpose=role | jq -r '.roles |  | @tsv' Connect the Slack channel. Have a workspace admin install the Pulumi Slack app. In Pulumi Cloud, link the account you’ll use to deploy the automation to your Slack identity under Account settings > Pulumi Agents. This lets Pulumi find channels in your workspace. Invite the app to your deployment channel and copy the channel ID from its details in Slack. Supply both IDs through ESC. Add the following to an ESC environment named deployment-agents/settings. The deployment-agents prefix on each key matches the project name in Pulumi.yaml. values: pulumiConfig: deployment-agents:agentRoleId: "<Pulumi Cloud role ID>" deployment-agents:slackChannelId: "<Slack channel ID>" From the deployment-agents project, import the environment into the selected stack and deploy: npm install @pulumi/pulumiservice@1.7.0 pulumi config env add deployment-agents/settings pulumi up pulumi up creates the Deployment Troubleshooter agent and the Investigate failed production updates automation. The automation begins watching checkout/prod. What the team sees in Slack In a live test on a disposable stack, the check-release-manifest resource ran a local command to verify that release-manifest.json existed. The file was absent, so the update failed. Pulumi posted the automation’s name in the deployment channel as soon as the investigation started. The agent then replied in the Slack thread with its diagnosis. check-release-manifest had failed with Missing release-manifest.json. title: [Docker] The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance
summary: The Agent Trust Gap The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a new security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs? A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system. The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary. Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened? In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do. There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below. Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Sandbox Policies: Where Can the Agent Operate? An agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them. Docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally. Network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction. For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own. A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent: $ sbx policy check network api.anthropic.com Allowed: api.anthropic.com $ sbx policy check network blocked.example.com Denied: blocked.example.com The important part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow. This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate? MCP Tool Governance: What Can the Agent Do? Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools. MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it. Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server: permit (principal, action == MCP::Action::"invokeTool", resource) when { resource in MCP::Server::"example" && resource.readOnly == true }; Here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server. This makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint. One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead. With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do? Audit + Visibility: Can We See What Happened? Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied. Docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses. Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows. Denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working. Current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available. That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened? A Trusted Software Supply Chain: Docker Hardened Images AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying? Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker. In practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built. For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself. AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on. Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance. Putting the Three Layers Together Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an issue, update a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way. The agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access. Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether. For governance activity currently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow. If that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime. The model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision. That is the practical value of the three layers working together: Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate. MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use. Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled. Taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently. Autonomy Without Unbounded Authority The challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions. That makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded. Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts. The goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority. As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more. title: [Amazon AWS] Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
summary: Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297 export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000. curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started make_bucket: local-getting-started $ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt $ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/ upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt $ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it back with get-item. $ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \ --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \ --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST $ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \ --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}' $ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the  section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions}; use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{ AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType, ScalarAttributeType, }; # async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default()); let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest()) .http_client(emulator.http_client()) .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1")) .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider()) .load() .await; let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config); ddb.create_table() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .attribute_definitions( AttributeDefinition::builder() .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S) .build().unwrap()) .key_schema( KeySchemaElement::builder() .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash) .build().unwrap()) .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest) .send().await.unwrap(); ddb.put_item() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())) .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into())) .send().await.unwrap(); let got = ddb.get_item() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())) .send().await.unwrap(); assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi"); } When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

title: [HashiCorp] Nomad in 2026: A Year of Scale, Security, and Ecosystem Velocity
summary:
The future of orchestration is heterogeneous. Platform teams should not have to choose between containers, raw binaries, and virtual machines, or maintain separate, siloed control planes for each. Today’s infrastructure demands an orchestration platform that pairs high-throughput scheduling with granular kernel-level security and clean operational automation across them. This year, engineering across the Nomad ecosystem has focused on advancing that foundation. Spanning the Nomad 2.0 and 2.1 release cycles, from core consensus and performance enhancements to new scheduling governance, runtime drivers, autoscaling, and Terraform tooling, Nomad continues to evolve to meet the demands of modern production environments. Improve control plane performance and recovery Nomad 2.0 lets operators migrate the Raft log store from BoltDB to a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) backend, which offers better performance for write-heavy workloads. Nomad 2.0.5 added the plan_apply_pipeline setting, which lets operators control how many outstanding plans the leader allows when evaluating plans. For recovery, Nomad 2.1 adds nomad operator snapshot filter. It removes selected entries from a snapshot and writes the result to a copy. Operators can use it to clean up a snapshot before restoring it, or to remove a large number of pending evaluations when recovering a cluster from an outage. Govern high-volume batch bursts with node pool queueing High-volume batch bursts, like automated pipelines or ML inference, can leave smaller jobs stuck behind larger ones when capacity runs short. Nomad 2.1 introduces the experimental Batch Job Queue to give operators greater control over how batch jobs are scheduled within node pools. The queue holds pending batch jobs and provides two queueing options, FIFO, and a dynamic priority implementation which adjusts the priority of queued jobs based on multiple configurable factors. This helps prevent tenant starvation and supports fair-share scheduling. Advance containerless security and storage with Driver exec2 exec2 v0.2.0 brings container-grade capabilities to non-containerized workloads, adding Linux ambient capabilities, Host and CSI volume mounts, and nomad alloc exec support without container daemon overhead. The exec2 task driver leverages native Linux kernel namespaces and Landlock filesystem sandboxing to isolate raw binary tasks. With v0.2.0, operators can selectively grant Linux ambient capabilities using allow_caps, cap_add, and cap_drop — a web service can bind privileged ports via CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE while dropping all other root privileges. exec2 tasks can now mount persistent storage via standard Nomad Host and CSI volume blocks, native nomad alloc exec support enables interactive shell debugging and script-based health checks, and memory telemetry transitions to modern Linux standards, accurately reporting Resident Set Size (RSS) under cgroups v2. Expand workload diversity with rootless Podman and virtual machines Orchestration flexibility extends beyond containers and binaries to include rootless environments and virtual machines: Rootless Podman (v0.6.5): Nomad Driver Podman 0.6.5 streamlines its dependency footprint by removing transitive Docker Go packages while adding multi-architecture platform overrides (os, arch, variant), direct HTTP(S) image archive loading, and shared IPC namespaces for inter-task /dev/shm communication. Virtual Machine Orchestration with Virt (Tech Preview): The Virt Task Driver v0.0.2-beta.1 (Tech Preview) advances native virtual machine orchestration on Nomad, adding support for host directory and Ceph storage pools, block-device volume attachments, and macvtap network interfaces. Strengthen infrastructure resilience with APM-driven autoscaling and fail-safe drains Effective autoscaling requires both application-aware metrics and fail-safe teardowns. Relying solely on CPU or memory thresholds often lags behind real traffic surges, while aggressive node scale-in risks terminating instances before draining tasks have fully stopped. Nomad Autoscaler v0.6.0 and v0.5.0 address both. New native APM plugins for Instana (v0.6.0) and InfluxDB (v0.5.0), alongside Prometheus instant query support (query_window = "instant"), let teams drive scaling decisions directly from application metrics. Schedule blocks let you define time-based windows to proactively warm capacity ahead of predictable events. On lifecycle safety, v0.6.0 fixes a critical gap: the autoscaler now waits until all tasks on a drained node have fully stopped before issuing termination commands, preventing long-running shutdown hooks or background workers from being interrupted prematurely. Simplify GitOps and eliminate state secrets with Terraform provider v2.6.1 Managing Nomad jobs declaratively with Terraform is standard practice for modern platform teams. Two friction points have consistently come up: sensitive ACL tokens and variables persisting in Terraform state files, and Terraform applies overwriting dynamic task replica counts managed by the Nomad Autoscaler. Terraform Provider v2.6.1 addresses both. Ephemeral Resources allow CI/CD pipelines to generate short-lived Nomad ACL tokens, client intro tokens, and variables on the fly, utilizing them during execution without storing sensitive secrets in permanent Terraform state. The preserve_counts parameter ensures that Terraform applies update job specifications, container images, and configurations without overwriting dynamic scaling counts established by the Nomad Autoscaler. Combined with new nomad_node and nomad_nodes data sources for dynamic topology inspection, platform teams achieve clean, conflict-free GitOps automation. Nomad ecosystem releases at a glance The following matrix summarizes the recent releases across the Nomad platform and ecosystem: Component Version Key Operational & Architectural Value Nomad Platform v2.1.1 / v2.0.5 Batch Job Queue, raft-WAL store, plan_apply_pipeline, Snapshot Filtering Nomad Autoscaler v0.6.0 / v0.5.0 Instana & InfluxDB APM plugins, scheduled scaling windows, safe node termination Driver exec2 v0.2.0 Ambient Linux capabilities, CSI & Host volume mounts, alloc exec Driver Podman v0.6.5 Multi-arch overrides, HTTP(S) image transport, shared IPC, streamlined dependencies Driver Virt v0.0.2-beta.1 Native VM orchestration (Tech Preview) - Ceph/directory storage pools, block storage, macvtap Terraform Provider v2.6.1 Ephemeral secret resources, preserve_counts for seamless autoscaling, node data sources

Get started with Nomad 2.1 These releases reflect our ongoing focus: providing platform engineering teams with a reliable, flexible orchestrator that scales smoothly across any workload type. title: [CNCF] How to support your app on Kubernetes environments you don’t control
summary: Running an application in Kubernetes is one thing, but supporting that application in Kubernetes environments your customers run is something else entirely. You don’t control the cluster configuration, its upgrade schedule, the surrounding tooling, or the process for investigating an incident. But customers will still look to you when your application won’t install, an upgrade breaks, or a workload behaves differently in their environment than they expected. That doesn’t mean customer-managed Kubernetes deployments can’t work, but it does mean support has to account for the variation you’ll see in real clusters. No Two Customer Environments Are Alike You’ll definitely have two customers (or more!) who both say they run Kubernetes and yet have very different environments. One may run a managed Kubernetes service in a public cloud. Another may operate its own infrastructure. They may use different Kubernetes versions, networking configurations, ingress controllers, storage classes, image registries, security policies, observability tools, or access controls. Those differences affect how your application deploys and how your team supports it. A chart that installs cleanly in your reference architecture may fail because a customer’s admission policies reject a required permission, their storage configuration doesn’t meet your application’s requirements, or their cluster runs a Kubernetes version you haven’t tested yet or no longer support. Unfortunately, your customer still experiences that as a problem with your application. That’s why your team needs a documented view of what the application requires from the cluster, and what falls outside the support boundary. At a minimum, customers need to know: Which Kubernetes versions and distributions you support Which permissions, policies, and cluster capabilities the application needs What networking, ingress, DNS, certificate, secret management, and storage configuration the application expects What resources the application needs to run reliably Which logs, events, metrics, and configuration details your support team will need during an escalation. With bonus points for providing commands directly. The goal isn’t to make every customer environment identical (you can’t). Instead, you need to define a supported operating model so every deployment doesn’t turn into a new discovery process for your customer support team. Customers Won’t Upgrade on Your Schedule Your application roadmap may assume customers will move to newer Kubernetes versions quickly. A quick reality check: most won’t. Customers have their own release schedules, validation processes, maintenance windows, compliance requirements, internal dependencies, and risk thresholds. Even when they want to upgrade, their platform team may have a long list of cluster add-ons, integrations, and workloads to validate first. Like any other software, Kubernetes and different components in its ecosystem change over time. APIs are deprecated and removed, version compatibility varies across control-plane and node components, and the upstream project supports release branches for only the three most recent minor releases. Your team needs a compatibility policy that answers a few basic questions: Which Kubernetes versions do you support today? Which versions are approaching the end of support? How much notice do customers get before you stop supporting a version? What does a customer need to do if an application release depends on a newer Kubernetes capability? Can you offer a documented workaround when a customer can’t upgrade immediately? If the answer to every compatibility problem is to update Kubernetes, customers will quickly find that your support isn’t aligned with how they operate. Your team needs to explain what’s incompatible, why it matters, and the easiest path to return to a supported configuration. Kubernetes Expertise Has to Be Customer-Facing A general application support team can’t diagnose every Kubernetes issue. When a product runs inside a cluster your customer manages, customer-facing teams need enough Kubernetes depth to identify where the problem really lives. That doesn’t mean every support employee has to operate production clusters. It does mean someone working directly with customers needs to understand the difference between an application issue, a deployment-configuration issue, and a cluster-level issue. For example, a pod stuck in Pending may point to unavailable capacity, resource requests that don’t fit on available nodes, a scheduling constraint, or a policy that prevents placement. An image pull failure may involve registry access, credentials, network connectivity, or image policy enforcement. Those details determine who needs to take the next action and what evidence they need to act on it. Your customer-facing team needs dedicated Kubernetes expertise that can: Ask for the right diagnostic information early Review Kubernetes events, pod status, and relevant logs Identify when a customer platform, security, networking, or infrastructure team needs to get involved Explain the issue in terms each stakeholder can act on Escalate to engineering with enough environmental context to investigate effectively Getting accurate answers to these questions matters because the person opening a support case may not own the cluster. The application team probably owns the deployment. A platform team probably owns Kubernetes. Security owns policies. Another infrastructure team may own networking, storage, or identity. Someone on your team needs to help move the issue between those groups. Build for Variation You can’t control every Kubernetes environment where customers run your application. You can control whether your support model treats that variation as expected or as a surprise. So make sure you have a plan for it by: Defining what you support. Documenting the requirements that matter. Testing the Kubernetes versions and deployment conditions you commit to supporting. Setting a clear upgrade and deprecation policy. Making Kubernetes expertise available during onboarding, deployment, escalation, and ongoing support. The support model changes when a provider manages the Kubernetes layer alongside the customer. Instead of troubleshooting an application across an unknown mix of cluster configurations, versions, networking, and add-ons, the provider and customer can work from a more clearly defined operating foundation.
