title: [CNCF] Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
summary: Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation. It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy. We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on. This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2. Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy. What the profile showed Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request, the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands. Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes: Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions. The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost: One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down. Why: the same object, converted once per policy The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them. That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies), where it should have been O(1). The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once. The fix: convert once per request The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it. Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand. Keeping policy behavior identical The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place. Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent. Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath. Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build. What changed The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies. Matched policiesAllocations beforeAllocations afterEngine time beforeEngine time after12,3278540.31 ms0.10 ms1637,0552,7184.91 ms0.16 ms64148,1318,67220.01 ms0.36 ms The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies. The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run. Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does. Image verification too The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change. How this compares to native admission policies With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce: At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms. Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison. The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead. That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did. The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment. Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology. The legacy engine, briefly The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there. We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6. The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next. The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code. This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it. What this does not fix The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design. Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented. Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open. Limitations Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server. Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd. The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded. The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set. Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active. Reproduce it The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context. If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers. Conclusion Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization. Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç, whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work. title: [Engineering at Meta] Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
summary: Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017. We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work. This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency. Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services. The Goal and What Makes It Difficult One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging: The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds. Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking, hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges. Capabilities of Intelligent Delivery 1. Request Understanding: A Shared ML Intelligence Layer for Compute Some ad requests benefit more from additional computation than others. Initially, we captured these differences through coarse segments: Requests were grouped by attributes such as surface, context, and ad creative representation, with engineers creating policies to allocate resources for each group. This approach delivered improvements but did not scale. Every new signal multiplied the rules, making the effort unsustainable, and independent segments could not capture the nonlinear interactions among thousands of signals, which limited accuracy. We achieved about a 20% improvement in identifying the highest-impact ad requests in offline benchmarks on major surfaces, relative to our previous production model, after reframing this into two ML problems: Which ad requests are most likely to benefit from additional compute? And how will different resource settings affect their outcomes and serving performance? A side-by-side comparison of static rule-based segmentation, where every request in a bucket gets the same compute, and signal-driven decisions, where an ML-driven predictor sets compute for each request. To answer the first question, we built the Resource Core Model, deep learning models with 6B sparse parameters and 20M dense parameters that run once before candidate retrieval and are shared across the delivery funnel. Learned embeddings and deep feature interactions capture nuanced request patterns that manually defined segments cannot. We then fine-tune the Resource Core Model into a set of specialized models, each generating incremental signals about outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. Together this forms a shared ML intelligence layer for resource allocation: The Resource Core Model understands each request and its serving behavior, while individual mechanisms determine how to translate those predictions into actions. An architecture diagram of the Resource Core Model, showing how dense and sparse request features pass through stacked interaction layers to predict each request’s outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. 2. Allocation Mechanisms: A Hierarchy of Decision Engines Ads serving runs on a globally distributed, heterogeneous fleet with many data center regions, several hardware generations, and millions of hosts, all shared by a multi-tier serving stack. A single allocation mechanism cannot control the complex resource distribution end to end. So we decomposed the problem into a hierarchy of layers and built a dedicated decision engine for each. The easiest way to see the hierarchy is to follow a single request through it. Someone opens their feed. An ad request is created, and over the next few hundred milliseconds it passes through a chain of resource allocation decisions. This leads us to three important questions and answers. Which region serves it? Traffic and capacity are not colocated, and each region carries a different hardware mix and a different amount of headroom — so the same unit of compute is more efficient in some places than in others. We built real-time infrastructure to dynamically shift traffic between regions in a cycle of minutes, driving toward the point where every region achieves the same level of efficiency on its marginal unit of capacity. What hardware does it land on? Our fleet spans CPUs from Intel, AMD, and Arm and accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and our own Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), across several generations of each. The hard part isn’t the variety; it’s that capacity isn’t interchangeable. Our stages are bound by different resources — retrieval by memory capacity, ranking by compute, and model inference by accelerator throughput — so there is no single fastest SKU, only a best match per workload. We benchmark measured efficiency for every workload-SKU pair, then solve the assignment so that scarce hardware goes to the workloads that convert it into the most useful work. Inside the host, how much of this machine does the request get? Concurrent requests differ in latency budget and impact, under a hard tail-latency SLO. We predict each request’s expected outcome and its compute and latency cost in real time using our advanced deep learning models, and solve a constrained optimization that maximizes impact delivered within the host’s latency budget — as the host load increases, the performance trade-off rises and resource-intensive low-impact work is trimmed first. Enforcing those decisions takes control across the whole stack, so the framework spans from kernel-level scheduler up to application-level thread pools. A three-step flowchart following one ad request through the decision hierarchy: which region serves it, which hardware it runs on, and how much of the host it gets. These three steps are just a subset of the allocation decisions we make during a request’s lifecycle. Following this, we optimize the number of ads to rank for each request in each ranking stage, what ad candidates enter the pool, and much more. These allocation decisions are tightly coupled, so a resource change in any one of them ripples across the whole system. Shifting traffic between regions changes per-host load, which drives the feedback controller that sets how much work each request gets. We validate these changes in an end-to-end, closed-loop hardware testing environment to make sure we are optimizing for the global optimum instead of a local optimum. 3. Optimization Loop: Self-Optimizing Serving with Agentic AI As our ad system advances, productionizing a new model, a new mechanism, or new hardware into the system requires a lot of effort to achieve seamless integration. We can’t brute-force every single configuration across millions of tunable dimensions built in our system for a new change. That would require too much time and far more hardware resources than we have. We relied heavily on human expertise and engineers’ prior knowledge to identify promising configurations. But this approach didn’t scale, because every new model, mechanism, and hardware generation expanded the search space faster than engineers could explore it. We tried automating this with a constrained optimization approach, which delivered improvements but remained inflexible and slow. We found that it lacked the ability to generalize (it could only cover a few key knobs) and couldn’t effectively incorporate human intuition from prior experience. Instead of doing a blind search, AI agents continuously monitor the entire system landscape, identifying changes and inefficiencies to address. In a long context window, an agent reads mechanism source code, design documents, and a decade of experiment logs and narrows that to a handful of changes worth testing. Engineers review and approve the final change before it ships. Today, agents can already propose well-reasoned changes and design and run rigorous experiments. In the first half of 2026, agents contributed to about 20% of Intelligent Delivery optimizations. On our most automated mechanism, they now contribute to about 80% of the engineering effort, from understanding the system landscape and forming hypotheses to running experiments and converging on the final change. This shortens the optimization loop from months to weeks while keeping people firmly in control. And it steadily captures the expertise engineers have built over the years. A loop diagram of the AI-driven optimization cycle, where agents collect data, propose changes, and run experiments, with an engineer approving every change and a shared knowledge base feeding each step. The Next Frontiers for Intelligent Delivery End-to-end real-time optimization: Today, understanding a request and deciding how to serve it are still two separate steps. We’re building toward fusing them into a single model that reads a request and serves it in real time, without months of experiments. There’s established work in varying compute per request with learning-based methods. However, doing it jointly across every serving stage at once — under shifting traffic, hard capacity limits, and tight inter-stage dependencies — is the part that’s still open, and it’s what we’re pushing on. Serving state-of-the-art models on GPUs: Large ranking models, like Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM), are growing toward LLM scale and increasingly run on GPUs, which opens a different optimization space. GPU capacity doesn’t divide the way CPU time does — it comes in whole, fixed blocks, and throughput, batching, and memory all behave differently. The levers we built for a CPU world have to be reimagined, and much of our work now goes into understanding those mechanisms and turning them into new levers. The more useful work we get out of each accelerator, the more people we can serve with strong models under the same capacity. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)
summary: A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt. I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS. Headlines Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub. What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production. AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges. Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data. How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. title: [HashiCorp] Terraform introduces tfpolicy support for Stacks, SCIM support, and more
summary: Over the past quarter, the HashiCorp Terraform engineering team has introduced new capabilities that make infrastructure management more scalable, secure, and easier to automate. These updates help platform teams streamline large-scale deployments, simplify operations with AI-ready workflows, strengthen security and governance, and manage infrastructure more efficiently. The latest HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise improvements include: Terraform policy support for Stacks Multi-deployment group orchestration Agent-ready Terraform Stacks CLI SCIM user lifecycle management Terraform Policy Support for Stacks Feature gap: As organizations adopt Terraform Stacks to manage infrastructure at scale, platform teams need the same governance guardrails they rely on for standard workspaces. Extending Terraform policy, HashiCorp's native, HCL-based policy-as-code framework, to Stacks gives teams a consistent way to enforce compliance and security standards as they scale multi-account and multi-region deployments. What's new: We are excited to introduce the general availability (GA) of Terraform policy support for Stacks, available for HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise. Platform teams can now apply HCL-based policies against Stacks, extending governance across infrastructure deployments. HCP Terraform runs policy evaluations after each deployment plan completes and re-evaluates policies for every subsequent plan-and-apply cycle when deployments have deferred changes. Platform teams can scope Terraform policy sets to all Stacks and workspaces in an organization, to specific projects, or to individual Stacks, giving them the same fine-grained control they have with workspaces today. Benefits: • Consistent governance across Stacks and workspaces: Platform teams can enforce the same HCL-based policies across Stacks and standard workspaces, so security and compliance guardrails apply everywhere infrastructure is provisioned. • Early feedback in the deployment lifecycle: Because policies evaluate immediately after each deployment's plan, teams catch policy violations before changes are applied, reducing the risk of non-compliant infrastructure reaching production. • Familiar authoring experience: Since Terraform policy uses HCL, the same language as Terraform, practitioners can write, test, and version-control Stacks policies using workflows they already know. To learn more, check out the Policy enforcement for Stacks documentation. Multi-Deployment Group Orchestration Feature gap: As Terraform Stacks scales to support hundreds of deployments, platform teams need a safe and efficient way to coordinate rollouts across large infrastructure fleets. Prior to this enhancement, Custom Deployment Groups were limited to a one-to-one relationship with deployments, providing organizational structure but lacking the orchestration controls needed to manage rollout risk, concurrency, and visibility at scale. What's new: We are introducing the general availability of multi-deployment group orchestration for HCP Terraform Premium and Terraform Enterprise. Deployment groups now evolve into true orchestration primitives capable of coordinating multiple deployments as a single rollout unit. Teams can define a failure tolerance threshold to automatically limit rollout blast radius, use eager planning controls to delay large-scale plan generation until explicitly triggered, and monitor rollout progress through new group-level visibility and management experiences. Together, these capabilities allow customers to safely scale deployment operations from tens to hundreds of deployments while maintaining control and observability. Benefits: Safer large-scale rollouts: Failure tolerance automatically throttles rollout progression and, once the configured threshold is exceeded, stops applying additional deployments in the group, reducing the risk of widespread production impact. Improved operational efficiency: Eager planning controls help avoid excessive plan generation, API rate limiting, and resource contention in large environments. Centralized rollout management: Platform engineers can manage groups of deployments as a single unit, using aggregated status views and group-level actions to simplify operations. Enhanced visibility: Dedicated Deployment group views provide a consolidated picture of rollout health, including success, failure, and blocked deployment counts, making it easier to diagnose and recover from issues. To learn more, check out deployment runs documentation. Agent-Ready Terraform Stacks CLI Feature gap: As organizations increasingly adopt AI-assisted operations, platform teams need infrastructure workflows that can be executed, monitored, and debugged programmatically. Terraform Stacks has continued expanding its CLI experience to support these emerging automation patterns, making it easier for users and AI agents to operate Stacks within CI/CD pipelines and other headless environments. What's new: We are introducing the general availability of a significant expansion of the Terraform Stacks CLI focused on agent-ready workflows. New non-interactive commands enable deployment monitoring, diagnostics, deployment and configuration inspection, and artifact access directly from the CLI. New monitoring commands such as terraform stacks deployment-run watch and terraform stacks deployment-group watch provide real-time visibility into deployment execution directly from the CLI. We also introduced broader JSON output support, allowing commands to return structured, machine-readable results that integrate seamlessly with AI agents and automation tooling. These enhancements make it easier for users to monitor deployments, investigate failures, and interact with Terraform Stacks through a consistent CLI experience without relying on custom API integrations. Benefits: Built for AI agents and automation: Non-interactive commands and structured JSON responses make it easier for AI agents, CI/CD systems, and other automated workflows to operate Terraform Stacks programmatically. Enhanced deployment visibility: New CLI commands provide direct access to deployment, configuration, and deployment-step information, simplifying deployment monitoring and status investigation. Accelerated troubleshooting: Expanded diagnostics capabilities help engineers quickly identify and understand configuration preparation issues, deployment failures, and step-level errors. Simplified integrations: Structured JSON output support provides predictable, machine-readable outputs that can be consumed by automation platforms without custom API tooling. Improved developer experience: Common operational tasks such as monitoring deployment progress, inspecting deployment artifacts, and diagnosing failures are now accessible through intuitive CLI commands, reducing workflow complexity and improving productivity. To learn more, check out the Stacks CLI documentation. SCIM User Lifecycle Management Feature gap: Enterprise organizations rely on their identity provider as the source of truth for user provisioning and deprovisioning. With SAML SSO alone, removing a user from the IdP doesn't remove their access to HCP Terraform and active sessions and API tokens can persist, creating security risk and compliance gaps. Manually managing users and team memberships can be error-prone and slow. What's new: We are excited to announce the general availability of System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) 2.0 support for HCP Terraform Standard and Premium customers. This integration enables automated user lifecycle management through integration with enterprise identity providers, improving security and compliance by automating user provisioning, de-provisioning, and team membership synchronization. When a user is deprovisioned in your identity provider, their access is automatically revoked, including active sessions and API tokens. New users are created automatically and added to the right teams based on membership of groups in your identity provider. Team memberships stay in sync, ensuring access control aligns with your identity provider as the source of truth without manual intervention. Benefits: No manual account management: Team memberships are continuously synchronized. New users are created and added to the appropriate teams based on group membership. Access is revoked when a user is removed from your identity provider, including active sessions and API tokens. Faster onboarding: SCIM-provisioned accounts skip email verification, so new team members get access immediately. Audit-ready compliance: All SCIM-initiated actions are logged in your organization's audit trail. This gives security and compliance reviews complete visibility. To learn more, check out the SCIM provisioning documentation. Get started with HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise You can try many of these new features now. If you are new to Terraform, sign up for an HCP account to get started today, and also check out our tutorials. HCP Terraform includes a $500 credit that allows users to quickly get started using features from any plan, including HCP Terraform Premium. Contact our sales team if you’re interested in trying our self-managed offering: Terraform Enterprise. Interested to learn about all the releases across our portfolio? Whether a small update or major release, stay in the entire loop with our Hashicorp ILM Monthly Digest and the HCP Terraform Changelog.
